Class enumeration in mixture models

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Mixture models explain heterogeneity in a population by assuming that it consists of a small number of unobserved subpopulations, the latent classes, each with its own pattern of responses. In latent profile analysis the pattern is a set of means of continuous indicators, and in latent class analysis it is a set of response probabilities of categorical indicators. When observations are nested in groups, the groups themselves can differ. Course enrolments, for example, are nested within students, and one student may be engaged in most of their courses while another is engaged in few. A two-level model captures such differences with a second set of latent classes, the group classes. Each group class is a type of student, defined by the proportions of the student’s enrolments that fall in each profile. For a given number of classes, the model estimates how large each class is and what its response pattern looks like. The number of classes itself is an input to the estimation, and the model returns no estimate of it. The analyst fixes the number of profiles, and in a two-level model the number of group classes, before estimation, and every substantive conclusion of the analysis depends on that choice.

Choosing the number of classes is difficult because the usual tools for comparing models each fall short in a specific way. Fit alone always favours more classes, since a model with one more class can reproduce the smaller model and improve on it. The likelihood ratio test, which compares nested models in most settings, gives invalid p-values here. A model with k classes is a model with k + 1 classes in which one class has size zero, and at that edge of the parameter space the test statistic loses its usual reference distribution. Valid p-values then require simulating many data sets from the smaller model and refitting both models to each, which is slow when many candidates are compared. Information criteria avoid testing altogether and instead balance fit against a charge for every estimated parameter. The criteria differ in that charge, so the Akaike information criterion, with a light charge, tends to favour more classes than the Bayesian information criterion, with a heavier one.

Applied data raise further problems. In large samples even the Bayesian information criterion often keeps decreasing as classes are added, because small departures from the model become detectable and each new class absorbs some of them. The lowest value then falls on the largest model that was fitted, and the size of each improvement says more than the position of the minimum. In a two-level model the number of profiles and the number of group classes are chosen together, and the charge of the Bayesian information criterion depends on whether the sample size counts the students or their enrolments. Finally, a model can fit the data well and still separate its classes poorly, so that many enrolments or students sit between classes, and its estimate can be a local maximum of the likelihood that a different starting point would improve.

This document applies class enumeration to a two-level latent profile model. Every combination of the requested numbers of profiles and group classes is fitted with enumerate_classes(), and every fitted model is kept. Each candidate is described by its information criteria under both definitions of the sample size, by the decrease of a criterion with each added profile and each added group class, by the knee of each of these curves, by the certainty of its classification and by checks of its estimation. Selected candidates are then compared side by side. The chosen candidate is taken from the fitted candidates for further analysis.

The evidence is reported in full because no single statistic determines the number of classes. The criteria, the changes between candidates and the classification quality together show where additional classes stop improving the model. A choice made from this evidence can be stated, justified and reproduced from the reported tables.

library(latents)

Data

The examples use course_engagement, a data frame in long format with one row per course enrolment. It contains 1,422 enrolments of 106 students. Five measures of activity in each course serve as indicators: browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, reading of the forum, posting to the forum and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course, so a value of zero is the course average. The column student identifies the student to whom each enrolment belongs.

head(course_engagement)
#>   student course sequence browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance previous_grade

#> 5 disengaged     wavering

Enrolments are nested in students. The profiles therefore describe patterns of activity in a single course, and the group classes describe students by how their enrolments are distributed across those patterns.

Fitting the candidate models

The candidates are fitted with enumerate_classes() from the data, the indicators in vars and the group identifier in id. The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes give the numbers of classes to try, and one model is fitted for every combination of them. Here the numbers of profiles run from one to six and the numbers of group classes from one to four. The argument model sets the covariance structure of the profiles. The value "VVI" gives every profile its own variances and fixes the covariances at zero. Without model, the four basic structures are fitted for every combination.

The likelihood of a mixture model has several local maxima, so each model is estimated from several random starts and the solution with the highest likelihood is kept. The argument n_starts sets the number of starts. The example uses three starts per model to keep the computation short. Applied analyses use ten or more. The argument seed makes the starts reproducible.

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models

The result holds 24 fitted candidates. Each candidate is named by its numbers of profiles and group classes, so that profiles4_groups3 has four profiles and three group classes, and the name identifies the candidate in every function that follows. The 3 candidates with one profile and several group classes could not be estimated. Group classes are defined by differences in the distribution of profiles, and a model with a single profile has no such differences. These candidates remain in the table with the error that stopped them.

The table of candidates has one row per candidate and is returned by as.data.frame().

The columns fall into groups.

Columns Content
candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model Identity of the candidate
log_likelihood, n_parameters Fit and size
aic, kic, bic_*, sabic_*, caic_*, awe_*, icl_*, clc_* Information criteria
profile_entropy, group_entropy Relative entropy at each level
avepp_min, avepp_max, avepp_mean, avepp_below Average posterior probability of the profiles
group_avepp_min, group_avepp_max, group_avepp_mean, group_avepp_below Average posterior probability of the group classes
converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings, error Checks of the estimation

Information criteria

An information criterion is the deviance, minus twice the maximized log-likelihood, plus a charge for every estimated parameter. Lower values indicate a better balance of fit and complexity. In a two-level model the charge of several criteria depends on the sample size. Criteria ending in _groups count the 106 students as the independent units, and criteria ending in _individual count the 1,422 enrolments. An analysis uses one of the two conventions throughout.

The candidate at the minimum of each criterion:

get_results(models, "criteria")
#>    criterion  convention         candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16703
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4_groups4          4               4   VVI 16769
#> 3        bic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16852
#> 4        bic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 16973
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16661
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16823
#> 7       caic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16903
#> 8       caic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 17011
#> 9        awe      groups profiles3_groups2          3               2   VVI 17169
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups3          2               3   VVI 17398
#> 11       icl      groups profiles4_groups2          4               2   VVI 16881
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 17140
#> 13       clc      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16580
#> 14       clc individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16944

The criteria disagree. With students as the units, the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) is lowest for profiles4_groups3, the integrated completed likelihood (ICL) for profiles4_groups2 and the approximate weight of evidence (AWE) for profiles3_groups2. With enrolments as the units, BIC is lowest for profiles3_groups3. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) is lowest for profiles6_groups4, the largest candidate fitted, because its light charge per parameter keeps it decreasing across the whole range.

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, one line per number of group classes, with the lowest value of each criterion ringed.

plot(models)

A minimum at the largest number of profiles or group classes fitted shows that the criterion is still decreasing there. The range of the candidates is then widened until the minimum lies inside it. Any criterion can be plotted by name, and what = "all" plots every criterion.

plot(models, what = "bic_groups")

The tree plots how the profiles divide as more are added. Each profile of a model is linked to the profiles of the next model that receive its observations.

plot(models, what = "tree")

Change with each added class

When a criterion decreases across the whole range, the size of each decrease becomes the evidence. For every candidate, the table reports the decrease in BIC from the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group classes, and the decrease from the candidate with one group class fewer and the same number of profiles. A positive value means that the added class lowered the criterion. The argument using selects another criterion.

With three group classes, adding a third profile lowers BIC by 85 and adding a fourth lowers it by 22. Adding a fifth profile raises BIC by 27, which appears in the table as a negative decrease. The decreases are plotted for both directions, along the number of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

plot(models, what = "deltas")

The knee of such a curve is the point beyond which added classes bring small improvements. The Kneedle algorithm scales both axes of a curve to the unit interval, takes the straight line from its first point to its last, and defines the knee as the point furthest below that line. The knee is computed along the number of profiles for each number of group classes, along the number of group classes for each number of profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters.

get_results(models, "knees")

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is profiles4_groups3. The straight line ends at the largest candidate, so the knee depends on the range fitted. Without the largest candidate the knee is profiles3_groups3, which the table records in stable and note. Along the number of group classes with four profiles, the knee is profiles4_groups2.

The criterion over all candidates at once, as the distance of each from the lowest value:

plot(models, what = "heatmap")

Classification quality

Every observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class. Relative entropy summarizes these probabilities over all observations, from 0 when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1 when every observation belongs to one class with certainty. The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the observations assigned to it. An AvePP of 0.7 or 0.8 and above is commonly taken to indicate adequate separation. The table of candidates reports the lowest, highest and mean AvePP at each level and the number of classes below a cutoff, which is 0.8 by default and is set with cutoff.

plot(models, what = "diagnostics")

The AvePP of every class of every candidate, with its size and the relative entropy of its level:

For profiles4_groups3, the relative entropy is 0.74 for the profiles and 0.82 for the group classes. The lowest AvePP is 0.8 among the profiles and 0.87 among the group classes.

Checks of the estimation

A solution reached from several random starts is more credible than a solution reached once, because a single start may have stopped at a local maximum. An estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, such as a variance at its lower bound, indicates a model too complex for the data. A class that holds a very small share of the observations is also hard to interpret. The following plots report these checks for every candidate.

plot(models, what = "trust")

plot(models, what = "smallest")

All of the plots for choosing the number of classes are produced together with plot(models, what = "selection").

Comparing candidates

Selected candidates are placed side by side with compare_models(). Candidates are named as in the table, given by their numbers of classes, or selected by a number of profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from the lowest of the candidates compared and the BIC weight. The weight is exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized to sum to one, the approximate posterior probability of each candidate when all have equal prior probability.

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

compare_models(models, bic_groups_pick, icl_groups_pick, awe_groups_pick)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model              Profiles  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> -----------------  --------  -------------  --  --------  --------  -----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> profiles4_groups3         4              3  51  -8307.15  16852.14   0.00   1.000  18014.13     0.74       0.80      0           0.82             0.87  <- lowest BIC
#> profiles4_groups2         4              2  47  -8326.19  16871.57  19.43   0.000  18021.23     0.74       0.79      1           0.94             0.98
#> profiles3_groups2         3              2  35  -8364.52  16892.26  40.12   0.000  17640.46     0.79       0.85      0           0.94             0.98

The same candidates given by their numbers of classes, with labels:

compare_models(models, bic = c(4, 3), icl = c(4, 2), awe = c(3, 2))

Analysis of the chosen candidate

The example continues with profiles4_groups3, the candidate with the lowest BIC with students as the units. It is taken from the fitted candidates by name with get_candidate(). The numbers of classes give the same model, as in get_candidate(models, 4, 3).

chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen

The profiles are plotted as their means on the five indicators.

plot_profiles(chosen)

Each group class of students has its own distribution of the four profiles.

plot_prevalence(chosen)

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

diagnostics(chosen)

plot_diagnostics(chosen)

The profiles can be related to an outcome. The mean of previous_grade in each profile is estimated with three_step(), which corrects for the uncertainty of the classification with the BCH method.

three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class   Mean          95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  -----  --------------  -----  -----------
#>     1   0.17  [ 0.08,  0.27]  0.049       338.59
#>     2  -0.30  [-0.41, -0.18]  0.057       255.57
#>     3  -0.36  [-0.53, -0.20]  0.083       111.57
#>     4   0.32  [ 0.18,  0.45]  0.069       210.39

Testing two neighbouring candidates

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test compares two candidates that differ by one class. Data sets are simulated from the smaller candidate, both candidates are refitted to each, and the p-value is the share of simulated likelihood ratios at least as large as the observed one. The test below compares three and four profiles with three group classes. Nineteen simulated data sets keep the example short. With 19 simulations the smallest attainable p-value is 1/20 = 0.05, and applied analyses use 99 or more.

smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 3 profiles, 3 group classes; alternative: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> Observed statistic: 82.548767
#> p-value: 0.05 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0487) from 19 of 19 valid replicates
plot(test)

Other kinds of model

Latent class models

student_esm contains 2,582 momentary reports of students, with eight activities recorded as yes or no. Naming the indicators in categorical makes every candidate a latent class model, and the candidates are named with classes in place of profiles.

activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
lca_models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:2,
                                categorical = activities, n_starts = 5,
                                seed = 1)
lca_models

With two group classes the three-class model has the lower BIC. Its relative entropy is 0.56, and its least distinct class has an AvePP of 0.64. The classes of this model overlap strongly, which limits their interpretation.

Single-level models

Observations without groups are modelled with enumerate_lpa() for continuous indicators and enumerate_lca() for categorical ones. The candidates are named by their numbers of profiles or classes alone.

srl_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                                   "self_efficacy", "self_regulation",
                                   "test_anxiety"),
                            n_profiles = 1:8, model = "VVI", n_starts = 10,
                            seed = 1)

Several covariance structures

Several structures in model multiply the candidates, and the structure joins the name. The numbers of classes alone then match several candidates, so a candidate is named in full.

crossed_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies",
                                       "intrinsic_value", "self_efficacy",
                                       "self_regulation", "test_anxiety"),
                                n_profiles = 2:4, model = c("VVI", "EEE"),
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
crossed_models

Transition models

With time, every candidate is a latent transition model across the occasions, here the order of each student’s enrolments in sequence.

transition_models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                                       time = "sequence", n_profiles = 2:6,
                                       n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 3,
                                       seed = 1)
transition_models

Functions

Call Result
enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model) The fitted candidate models
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate with every column
get_results(models, “criteria”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = 0.9) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Kneedle knee of each line, its range and its stability
plot(models), plot(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Information criteria across the candidates
plot(models, what = “tree”) Division of profiles as more are added
plot(models, what = “entropy”, “avepp” or “diagnostics”, cutoff = ) Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
plot(models, what = “deltas”, “heatmap”, “smallest” or “trust”, using = ) Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks
plot(models, what = “selection”) All of the plots for choosing the number of classes
get_candidate(models, “profiles4_groups3”), get_candidate(models, 4, 3) One fitted candidate
compare_models(models, “name”, c(4, 2), …) Named candidates side by side
compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = ) All candidates with the given numbers of classes
compare_models(name = fit, name = fit) Fitted models side by side, on the same data
get_candidate(comparison, “name”) The model behind a row of a comparison
get_results(comparison, “classification”) Every class of every compared model
